title: Cylinder Volume: V = πr²h
preview: Open the file cabinet with circle area, then thin-slice cylinder volume — vary r, vary h, then both, all using V = πr²h.

body.goal: Students see that cylinder volume is just circle area × height, by varying r and h one at a time. The formula stops being something to memorize and starts being something they can derive.
body.launch: Run the warm-up first (circle area). Then post the stem (V = πr²h) and start the slice. Use exact answers in terms of π — don't push to decimals unless time allows.
body.prerequisiteLabel: Warm up by computing circle areas before stacking them into cylinders.

prerequisiteSteps.problem: Area of a circle with r = 2
prerequisiteSteps.teacherNote: Anchor: A = πr². Most groups know this.

prerequisiteSteps.problem: Area of a circle with r = 3
Area of a circle with r = 5
Area of a circle with r = 10
prerequisiteSteps.teacherNote: Stress: r is squared, not doubled. The big jump is on purpose.

steps.teacherNote: Double the height — what happens to the volume? Discuss.
Height of 1 — volume equals the base area.
Now r changes. Pause: 'When we doubled h, V doubled. We just changed r from 2 to 3 — what did V do?'
Big r jump — r squares, so the growth is dramatic.
Both varied. Some groups will compute base × height; some will scale from a prior step.
Fractional radius — (1/2)² is 1/4, then × 4 gives 1. Watch for groups who forget to square the fraction.
Diameter, not radius — convert first. The classic test trap.

body.consolidation: Ask: 'When we double the height, what happens to V? When we double the radius, what happens to V?' Get to the rule: doubling h doubles V; doubling r quadruples V. Anchor that to V = πr²h — h is linear, r is squared.
